new_statements.quote: [pp.7-8] Stress patterns differ to a small degree between the Kuwarrangu and Warranganku dialects. As discussed in §2.3, Jingulu typically stresses the penultimate syllable, while Pama-Nyungan languages stress the initial. Some three-syllable words which Warranganku speakers stress on the second syllable (e.g. damángka 'head') are stressed on the first syllable by Kuwarrangu speakers (dámangka). [p.37] ... Aside from its use in the local Pama-Nyungan language Mudburra, ... In addition to borrowings, speakers of the Kuwarrangu dialect often pronounce words with the Pama-Nyungan initial stress pattern which speakers of the Warranganku dialect pronounce with penultimate stress (as mentioned in §1.1.4).
new_statements.citation: Pensalfini, Rob. 2003. A grammar of Jingulu, an Aboriginal language of the Northern Territory (Pacific Linguistics 536). Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, ANU.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Indirect only: the Jingulu grammar attributes an initial-stress pattern to 'Pama-Nyungan languages', naming Mudburra as the local Pama-Nyungan language whose bilingual (Kuwarrangu, Jingili-Mudburra) speakers carry initial stress into Jingulu; i.e. Mudburra is treated as a word-initial-stress language, consistent with Ngumpin-Yapa generally. No Mudburra-specific rule, no statement on long vowels, secondary stress or coverb+verb complexes.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about word-level stress as heard in Jingulu words pronounced by Mudburra-Jingulu bilinguals; not a description of Mudburra citation forms. A first-hand Mudburra statement almost certainly sits in Osgarby 2019 ch.1 ('phonological preliminaries') and in the 2019 dictionary's grammar guide, neither of which could be opened from our machine.
new_statements.identity_note: The only quotable passage (Pensalfini 2003) is from a grammar of Jingulu (jing1260, Mirndi, non-Pama-Nyungan) and concerns the 'Kuwarrangu' varieties spoken in mixed Jingili-Mudburra households at Elliott/Marlinja, i.e. the Eastern Mudburra contact zone; it characterises 'Pama-Nyungan languages' (with Mudburra named as the local one) as initial-stressing, not Mudburra directly. Osgarby 2019 covers both Eastern (Elliott/Marlinja) and Western (Top Springs, 'Kuwirrinji') Mudburra.

sources.note: Jingulu grammar; pp.7-8 (sec. 1.1.4) and p.37 (sec. 2.3): Jingulu stresses the penult 'while Pama-Nyungan languages stress the initial'; Kuwarrangu (mixed Jingili-Mudburra) speakers use 'the Pama-Nyungan initial stress pattern'; Mudburra named as 'the local Pama-Nyungan language'. Indirect evidence for Mudburra initial stress only.
